analysis.one_liner: Holds private equity firms liable for debts of companies they buy and ends carried interest tax breaks.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 6 cosponsors in November 2024, the bill never received a hearing or a vote in the Senate Finance Committee before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make buyout funds legally responsible for the debts, pension shortfalls, and legal penalties of the companies they take over, and would bar funds from paying themselves large dividends in the four years after a buyout. It would rewrite bankruptcy rules so laid-off workers, owed wages, severance, and gift card holders get paid ahead of insiders, cap executive bonuses in bankruptcy, and add protections for striking workers. It would also raise taxes on the industry by ending the carried interest tax break and taxing the management fees private funds collect from the companies they control.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies owned by private equity funds — about 12 million people per the bill's own findings — would gain the most: they could recover unpaid wages and severance ahead of other creditors in bankruptcy, and their employers' owners could be held personally liable for pension and layoff liabilities. Pension funds and other investors in private funds would get new fee and return disclosures and fiduciary protections. Consumers holding gift cards from bankrupt retailers would get up to $1,800 in priority. Patients at nursing homes and other care providers would be shielded from a financing structure that strips property into real estate investment trusts. Workers on strike could no longer be permanently replaced.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, pension savers, and bankrupt companies' creditors

how_it_helps.text: Makes a private fund that buys control of a company jointly and severally liable for all of that company's debts and legal penalties, including pension withdrawal liabilities, unfunded pension obligations owed to the federal pension insurer, and violations of worker-notice (WARN Act) law — so the fund, not workers or the pension system, absorbs the losses when a buyout fails.

Bars a company from paying dividends, buybacks, or other distributions to its private equity owner for four years after a buyout, and voids transfers that violate the limit — with employees and creditors allowed to sue to claw the money back, plus attorney's fees.

Rewrites bankruptcy law to move workers up the repayment line: wage priority doubles from $10,000 to $20,000, severance pay and benefit-plan contributions get priority status, back pay and labor-law penalties count as administrative expenses, and courts must weigh job preservation when approving sales of a company.

Cracks down on executive pay in bankruptcy: bonus and retention payments to insiders, senior executives, and the 20 next-highest-paid employees require court approval based on clear and convincing evidence, and are barred outright if the company cut severance for its regular workforce in the past year.
Gives consumers holding unredeemed gift cards from a bankrupt retailer up to $1,800 in priority repayment, so they are not left with worthless plastic when stores close.

Raises taxes on the industry: a surtax effectively equal to the top income tax rate applies to fees private funds collect from companies they control, leverage-heavy portfolio companies lose part of their interest deduction, and carried interest — fund managers' profit share now taxed at capital-gains rates — would be taxed as ordinary income.

Cuts off Medicare and Medicaid payments to health care providers that sell their buildings to or borrow against them with a real estate investment trust, and repeals the REIT tax rules that encourage hospitals and nursing homes to convert into landlord-tenant structures.
Makes it an unfair labor practice to permanently replace striking workers, to lock out employees before a strike, or to force workers to attend anti-union campaign activities.

Requires private funds that take federal or state money to disclose their owners, workforce demographics, CEO-to-worker pay ratio, and jobs saved, and blocks them from acquiring companies or paying shareholders for two years afterward; funds must also disclose fees and returns and can no longer require investors to waive fiduciary duties. Pension funds are expressly carved out of the new control-person liability.

analysis.who_pays: Private equity and hedge fund managers pay directly: their management fees would be surtaxed, their profit share taxed as ordinary income, and they would shoulder personal-scale liability for portfolio company failures. Secured lenders and other financial creditors would be repaid after workers in bankruptcies, and the pool of collateral available to them would be tapped first for unpaid wages. Health care real estate investment trusts would lose a tax-advantaged model of buying provider property. Broadly, buyout financing would get more expensive and some deals would not happen — a cost spread across companies seeking capital and the investors who fund buyouts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers, lenders

drawbacks.text: Joint and several liability for everything a portfolio company owes — plus a 5% control threshold and a 15-year lookback for clawing back buyout-related transfers — could make funds reluctant to buy struggling companies at all, reducing the rescues and turnarounds that buyout capital sometimes provides and raising the cost of capital for all acquired firms.

The four-year ban on shareholder distributions after a buyout, and the rule barring companies from relocating work overseas after a layoff, would restrict how owners can deploy their own capital and could push deals toward structures outside the bill's definitions.

The striking-worker provision would outlaw permanent replacements and pre-strike lockouts — a major change to federal labor law that employers argue removes their principal source of bargaining leverage, and it reaches far beyond the bill's private equity subject matter.

Moving wages, severance, and gift cards ahead of secured lenders in bankruptcy would make lending to risky companies more expensive, a cost that could be passed back to borrowers in the form of higher rates or tighter credit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers and communities that absorb the damage when a heavily indebted buyout collapses — lost jobs, unpaid wages, broken pensions — the bill offers real, concrete recovery rights that do not exist today, and its tax provisions close preferences that only investment managers use. The honest cost is economic: liability that follows the fund everywhere, a distribution ban, and lender subordination would make leveraged acquisitions riskier and more expensive, and some marginal deals — including rescues of genuinely failing firms — would not get done. The bill's breadth (it bundles labor law, bankruptcy, tax, health care, and securities rules) made it a statement bill rather than a calibrated one, which is part of why it drew no traction in committee.

outcome.mechanism: Warren introduced the bill in the Senate's final weeks; the Finance Committee never took it up, and it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the Stop Wall Street Looting Act on November 18, 2024, with six Senate cosponsors — five Democrats and one independent — all from her party's side of the aisle.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, which has jurisdiction over the tax provisions at its core.

No further action appears in the record: the committee held no hearing or markup, the full Senate never debated it, and no vote was ever taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity and hedge fund managers are better off, because the liability rules, dividend limits, fee surtax, and carried interest repeal never became law. Executives of bankrupt companies also keep the current, looser rules on bonus and retention pay.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity funds and their managers

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill, her third version of the Stop Wall Street Looting Act across Congresses.

for.name: 5 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Tammy Baldwin, Sherrod Brown, Jeff Merkley, Tina Smith, Ed Markey)

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (Chair: Sen. Ron Wyden, D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — in the six weeks between referral and the end of the Congress.

against.name: Private equity industry (American Investment Council and major buyout firms)
against.what_they_did: Opposed the Stop Wall Street Looting Act and its earlier versions, arguing liability and tax provisions would damage capital formation.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors were Democrats or the chamber's independent, with no Republican cosponsor; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call shows where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill's central target: funds would face full liability for portfolio company debts and penalties, a four-year ban on post-buyout distributions, clawback suits with a 15-year lookback, and a surtax on the fees they collect from companies they control. Its own findings cite retail bankruptcies like Sears, Toys "R" Us, and Payless as the harm the bill aims at.

Carried interest would be taxed as ordinary income instead of at capital-gains rates, and management fees collected from controlled companies would be surtaxed — eliminating the core tax advantages of the compensation model.

industries.industry: Health care real estate investment trusts
industries.note: Providers that sell their property to or borrow against it with a REIT would lose Medicare and Medicaid payments, and the special REIT tax rules for health care property and the REIT dividend deduction would be repealed — dismantling the sale-leaseback financing model in nursing homes and hospitals.

industries.industry: Corporate debt securitizers and private credit lenders
industries.note: The bill imposes risk retention requirements on securitization of corporate debt, so lenders packaging risky corporate loans would have to keep a slice of the losses they currently pass to investors.

Pension funds are exempted from the new control-person liability, and all fund investors gain mandatory fee and return disclosures plus a ban on waiving fiduciary duties — protections aimed at the roughly 12 million workers whose employers, pensions, landlords, or hospitals sit behind private fund ownership.
